summary: Defines the second version of the Remote Network Monitoring MIB, which lets network monitoring devices report on traffic seen on a network. It extends monitoring beyond the link layer to higher protocols. It was replaced by RFC 4502.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines the second version of the management information base for remote monitoring probes. A probe is a device that sits on a network and counts what passes by; this version lets it report on protocols up to the application layer, and sets out how several management stations share one probe.

subtitle: The second generation of remote network monitoring: probes that report traffic by protocol, all the way up to the application layer.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to see what is happening on their networks, but the first version of the remote monitoring MIB only looked at the link layer, and a probe that reports everything a network carries has to cope with several management stations using it at once.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the second-generation MIB module, grouped into nine groups that a probe implements wholesale, with control tables that are written to configure a measurement and data tables that are read to get the results, plus an ownership mechanism for sharing the probe's resources.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2021 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 4502.

sections.title: The Network Management Framework
sections.content:
The Internet-standard Network Management Framework consists of three components. RFC 1902 defines the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management. RFC 1213, STD 17, defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols. RFC 1905 defines SNMP, the protocol used for network access to managed objects. The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.

Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base, or MIB. Within a given MIB module, objects are defined using the SMI's OBJECT-TYPE macro. At a minimum, each object has a name, a syntax, an access-level and an implementation-status.

The name is an object identifier, an administratively assigned name which specifies an object type. The object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object, and for human convenience a textual string, the object descriptor, is often used as well. The syntax defines the abstract data structure corresponding to the object type, using ASN.1, though RFC 1902 purposely restricts the ASN.1 constructs which may be used, explicitly for simplicity. The access-level defines whether it makes protocol sense to read and/or write the value of an instance of the object type, independently of any administrative authorization policy. The implementation-status indicates whether the object is mandatory, optional, obsolete or deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP management rests on three pieces: a way to name things, a standard set of core objects, and a protocol for reading and writing them over the network.

sections.title: What Remote Monitoring Is For
sections.content:
The RFC continues the architecture created by the RMON MIB of RFC 1757 by providing a major feature upgrade, primarily by providing RMON analysis up to the application layer.

Remote network monitoring devices, often called monitors or probes, are instruments that exist for the purpose of managing a network. Often these probes are stand-alone devices and devote significant internal resources for the sole purpose of managing a network. An organization may employ many of these devices, one per network segment, to manage its internet. In addition, these devices may be used by a network management service provider to access a client network, often geographically remote.

The objects defined in the document are intended as an interface between an RMON agent and an RMON management application, and are not intended for direct manipulation by humans. While some users may tolerate the direct display of some of these objects, few will tolerate the complexity of manually manipulating objects to accomplish row creation, so those functions should be handled by the management application.

Five goals are set out. Offline operation: a management station will sometimes not be in constant contact with its remote monitoring devices, sometimes by design to lower communications costs, especially over a WAN or dialup link, or by accident as network failures affect the communications. The MIB therefore allows a probe to be configured to perform diagnostics and collect statistics continuously, even when communication with the management station may not be possible or efficient, and to attempt to notify the station when an exceptional condition occurs. Proactive monitoring: given the resources available, it is helpful for the monitor to run diagnostics and log network performance continuously, so it is always available at the onset of any failure and can store historical information for later playback. Problem detection and reporting: the monitor can be configured to recognise conditions, most notably error conditions, and continuously check for them, logging the event and notifying management stations in a number of ways. Value added data: because the probe is located directly on the monitored portion of the network, it can add significant value to the data it collects, for instance by highlighting the hosts that generate the most traffic or errors. Multiple managers: an organization may have multiple management stations for different units or functions and for disaster recovery, so the device has to deal with more than its own management station, potentially using its resources concurrently.
sections.plainLanguage: The probe is designed to keep working when the management station cannot, and to keep a record of what happened so a failure can be understood later.

sections.title: The Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The objects are arranged into nine groups: protocol directory, protocol distribution, address mapping, network layer host, network layer matrix, application layer host, application layer matrix, user history, and probe configuration.

These groups are the basic units of conformance. If a remote monitoring device implements a group, it must implement all objects in that group; for example, a managed agent that implements the network layer matrix group must implement the nlMatrixSDTable and the nlMatrixDSTable. Implementations of this MIB must also implement the system and interfaces group of MIB-II, and MIB-II may also mandate the implementation of additional groups. The groups exist to provide a means of assigning object identifiers and a method for managed agents to know which objects they must implement.

The document also contains enhancements to tables defined in the RMON MIB. It adds the DroppedFrames and LastCreateTime conventions to each table defined in the RMON MIB. It augments the RMON filter table with a mechanism that allows filtering based on an offset from the beginning of a particular protocol, even if the protocol headers are of variable length. And it augments the RMON filter and capture status bits with additional bits for WAN media and generic media.

Those new status bits are defined in the RFC. Bit 6 is for WAN media and is set for packets coming from one direction and cleared for packets coming from the other; which direction gets which value is an implementation specific matter, but it must be consistent for all packets received by the agent, and if the agent knows which end of the link is local and which is network, the bit should be set for packets from the local side and cleared for the network side. Bit 7 is for any media and is set for any packet with a physical layer error. Bit 8 is for any media and is set for any packet too short for the media. Bit 9 is for any media and is set for any packet too long for the media.

These enhancements are implemented by RMON-2 probes that also implement RMON, and do not add any requirements to probes that are compliant to just RMON.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe picks the groups it implements, and each group has to be implemented whole. The second version also extends the tables from the first version rather than replacing them.

sections.title: Controlling the Probe and Sharing It
sections.content:
Because of the complex nature of the available functions, they often need user configuration, and in many cases a function requires parameters to be set up before a data collection operation can proceed. Many functional groups in this MIB have one or more tables in which to set up control parameters, and one or more data tables in which to place the results of the operation. The control tables are typically read and write, while the data tables are typically read only.

Because the parameters in the control table often describe resulting data in the data table, many of them can be modified only when the control entry is not active. The method for modifying them is to de-activate the entry, perform the SNMP Set operations, and then re-activate it. Deleting the control entry deletes any associated data entries, which also gives a convenient method of reclaiming the resources the data used.

Some objects provide a mechanism to execute an action on the device as a result of a change in the object's state. For those objects, a request to set an object to the same value it currently holds causes no action to occur.

Because resources on a probe are scarce and typically allocated when control rows are created by an application, and many applications may use a probe simultaneously, the document provides the OwnerString mechanism for each management station initiated function. Each function has a label identifying the initiator, or owner, and the initiator sets it so that a management station can recognise resources it owns and no longer needs, so that an operator can find the station that owns a resource and negotiate for it to be freed, or unilaterally free it, and so that a station can, upon initialisation, recognise resources it reserved in the past and free them if it no longer needs them. Management stations and probes should support any format of the owner string dictated by local policy; it is suggested the name contain one or more of the IP address, management station name, network manager's name, location or phone number. Functionality the device or the probe's administrator wishes to set up is owned by the device itself or by the administrator and is intended to be long-lived, in which case the relevant owner object is set to a string starting with 'monitor'. Indiscriminate modification of monitor-owned configuration by network management stations is discouraged.

Row addition uses the RowStatus method described in RFC 1903. The agent must check the parameters to make sure they are appropriate given the restrictions in this MIB and any implementation specific restrictions such as lack of resources, and there are two opportunities to do so: when the management station sets each parameter object, or when it sets the row status object to active. If the latter is chosen it would be unclear to the station which of the several parameters was invalid and caused the badValue error, so wherever possible the implementor should choose the former. To guard against collisions when two managers try to create the same conceptual row at the same time, each such control entry contains a status object with special semantics: an attempt to create a status object that already exists returns an error, and only the first of several simultaneous attempts succeeds.
sections.plainLanguage: You switch a measurement on, configure it, and switch it on again. Every measurement carries a label naming who asked for it, so a probe can tell two operators apart and can be told to release what one of them no longer needs.

sections.title: The Protocol Directory and Limited Extensibility
sections.content:
Every RMON 2 implementation will have the capability to parse certain types of packets and identify their protocol type at multiple levels. The protocol directory presents an inventory of the protocol types the probe is capable of monitoring, and allows the addition, deletion and configuration of protocol types in that list.

One concept deserves special attention: the limited extensibility of the protocol directory table. The RMON 2 model is that protocols are detected by static software that has been written at implementation time. As a matter of configuration, an implementation does not have the ability to suddenly learn how to parse new packet types. However, an implementation may be written such that the software knows where the demultiplexing field is for a particular protocol, and can be written in such a way that the decoding of the next layer up is table-driven. This works when the code has been written to accommodate it, and can be extended no more than one level higher.

The RFC's example makes this concrete. Suppose an implementation has C code that understands how to decode IP packets on any of several ethernet encapsulations, and also knows how to interpret the IP protocol field to recognize UDP packets and how to decode the UDP port number fields. That implementation may be table-driven so that among the many different UDP port numbers possible, it is configured to recognize 161 as SNMP, port 53 as DNS, and port 69 as TFTP. The limited extensibility of the protocol directory table would then allow an SNMP operation to create an entry that creates an additional table mapping for UDP that recognizes UDP port 123 as NTP and begins counting such packets.

This limited extensibility is an option that an implementation can choose to allow or disallow for any protocol that has child protocols.

The document also explains how errors are counted. Packets with link-level errors are not counted anywhere in this MIB, because most variables in the MIB require decoding the contents of the packet, which is meaningless if there is a link-level error. Packets in which protocol errors are detected are counted for all protocols below the layer in which the error was encountered, so packets with errors detected at the network layer are not counted anywhere in this MIB, while packets with errors detected at the transport layer may have network-layer statistics counted.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe cannot be taught a new protocol while it is running, but it can be told to recognise one more port number in a protocol it already understands.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is short and specific. In order to implement this MIB, a probe must capture all packets on the locally-attached network, including packets between third parties. Those packets are analysed to collect network addresses, protocol usage information and conversation statistics. Data of this nature may be considered sensitive in some environments, and in such environments the administrator may wish to restrict SNMP access to the probe.

A probe implementing this MIB is likely to also implement RMON, which includes functions for returning the contents of captured packets, potentially including sensitive user data or passwords. It is recommended that SNMP access to these functions be restricted.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe sees everything on the wire, so access to it should be limited to the people who are allowed to see that.

THE FIVE GOALS OF REMOTE NETWORK MONITORING

items.title: Offline operation
items.text: The probe keeps diagnosing and collecting statistics even when it cannot reach the management station.

items.title: Proactive monitoring
items.text: The monitor is always available at the onset of a failure and can store history for later diagnosis.

items.title: Problem detection and reporting
items.text: The probe is configured to recognise conditions, log them, and notify management stations.

items.title: Value added data
items.text: The probe sits on the network it watches, so it can point at the hosts causing most traffic or errors.

items.title: Multiple managers
items.text: The probe has to share its finite resources among several management stations at once.
